prompt: What separates a request's headers from its body?
hint: It is the part of the request you cannot see.

choices.text: A line with a single full stop
choices.why: That convention belongs to another protocol; HTTP does not use it.

choices.text: An empty line on its own
choices.why: One empty line, and everything after it is content.
It says how long the body is, not where the headers end.
A request may carry any headers at all, so there is nothing to count to.

prompt: A response opens with `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`. What does changing `OK` to something else affect?
hint: Ask which part of that line software reads.

choices.why: Nothing checks the phrase, so nothing would report anything differently.
The number is the contract; the phrase is for whoever is reading.
A cache key is built from the address and the headers it was told about.

choices.text: The browser shows the new word
choices.why: The phrase does not reach the page; it stays in the response line.

prompt: Fill the blank: because HTTP is ___, a server is not obliged to remember anything between two requests, and the next one can be answered by a different machine.
hint: It is the property that let the web scale sideways.

prompt: Put the parts of a request in the order they are sent.
hint: One of the four is invisible.
items: The start line: the method, the path and the version
The body, if there is one
trap: The usual slip is leaving out the blank line, because it has nothing in it. It is the part that tells the far end the headers are finished, and without it the server waits for a header that is not coming.

prompt: Why did the `Host` header have to exist?
hint: The address found a machine. What did it not find?

choices.text: One machine answers for many names
choices.why: One line of text turned one address into as many sites as you like.

choices.text: Caches need the name to store it
choices.why: Caches file by address, and did so before this header existed.
Language is negotiated with a different header entirely.
Routers read addresses, four layers below anything named here.

prompt: What does it mean for a method to be idempotent?
hint: It is about repeating it, not about changing things.

choices.text: Doing it twice leaves the same state
choices.why: Set the price to ten twice, and the price is ten.
That is safe, which is a different property and a stronger one.
It has no relationship to who is allowed to send it.
The response may differ; it is the effect on the world that repeats harmlessly.

prompt: Match each method to what it asks for.
hint: Two of them ask without wanting a body back.

pairs.right: A copy of the thing at this address
The headers a copy would come with, and no content
This thing placed here, replacing what was there
The thing at this address removed

right_distractors: A list of everything under this address
A copy, and lock it while I hold it

prompt: An administration page puts its delete actions behind ordinary links. What eventually happens?
hint: Ask what follows links without being asked to.

choices.text: A crawler or a prefetch follows them
choices.why: It has happened to real applications, overnight, with nobody logged in.
Browsers have no idea what is behind a link and render it like any other.
The protocol describes the promise and does not police it.
They do work, which is the problem: they work for whoever visits them.

prompt: Fill the blank: `GET` and `HEAD` are called ___ methods, because they are not meant to change anything, which is why a browser may fetch them before you have clicked.
hint: The other property is idempotent.

prompt: A request times out with no answer. For which methods can the client simply send it again? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ask which ones survive being done twice.

choices.why: Safe, so a second attempt changes nothing.
Setting the same value twice leaves the same value.
The thing is gone after one attempt and after two.
A second attempt may charge the card a second time.
Adding one to a counter twice adds two.

prompt: A dashboard shows a sudden wall of `404`s and a separate wall of `500`s. Which one is yours?
hint: The first digit says whose fault it is.

choices.why: A failure is not the same as your failure, and the families exist to say so.
`4xx` is the caller asking wrong; `5xx` is you breaking.
A missing page is usually a stale link somebody else is following.
Rate matters for urgency; the family still says who is holding the problem.

prompt: An interface answers `200` with an error message in the body. What breaks?
hint: Think about the software between you and the caller.

choices.why: The caller can, and the four things between you and it cannot.

choices.text: Caches store it, retries do not fire
choices.why: Everything in the middle reads the number and nothing else.
A browser accepts any body with any code; it is told what it is by the type.
The length is whatever the body is; nothing about this changes it.

prompt: Match each code to what it says.
hint: Two of them are about who you are.

pairs.right: I do not know who you are — say, and try again
I know who you are, and no
There is nothing at this address
Slow down; a header says by how much

right_distractors: The thing you asked about has moved permanently
Somebody changed it since you last read it

prompt: Fill the blank: a proxy that never received an answer from the server behind it reports `___ Gateway Timeout`.
hint: It is in the 500 family, and one past 503.

prompt: Why might an application answer `404` for a document the caller is not allowed to see?
hint: Ask what a refusal reveals.

choices.why: That case is `401`; `403` is a refusal of somebody it recognises.

choices.text: A refusal would confirm it exists
choices.why: The price is that your own logs no longer distinguish the two.
Browsers render whatever body arrives, for both codes alike.

choices.text: A `403` would be cached along the way
choices.why: Caching is decided by the caching headers, not by which code was sent.

prompt: A page arrives and the browser shows the markup as visible characters instead of drawing it. What is wrong?
hint: The bytes are fine. Something described them.

choices.text: It was declared as plain text
choices.why: The browser did what it was told; what it was told was wrong.
Browsers repair broken markup rather than giving up and printing it.
A wrong encoding damages accented letters, and the tags still work.
A short length truncates the end, and the beginning still renders.

prompt: A response body of twelve visible characters, several of them accented, is sent with `Content-Length: 12`. What happens?
hint: The header is counted in bytes.

choices.text: The receiver waits for bytes never coming
choices.why: An accented letter is more than one byte, so twelve characters exceed twelve bytes.

choices.text: No harm; the header is advisory
choices.why: It is not advisory, and modern connections stay open for the next request.

choices.text: The accents arrive as question marks
choices.why: A length does not change an encoding; that is a different header's parameter.

choices.text: The body is cut at twelve
choices.why: The sender sends what it has; nothing trims it to match the claim.

prompt: Fill the blank: the header that says what the bytes of a body actually are — `text/html`, `application/json`, `image/png` — is `Content-___`.
hint: Without it, nothing downstream knows what it is holding.

prompt: Which of these are true about header names and values? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three of them will save you an afternoon each.

choices.text: The names ignore case, so `content-type` and `Content-Type` are the same header
choices.why: Different software has capitalised them differently for thirty years.

choices.text: A header may appear more than once, and for most of them that is a list
choices.why: `Set-Cookie` is the famous exception, which is why cookies are awkward.

choices.text: Servers cap the total size of the headers, often near eight kilobytes
choices.why: And the thing that grew past it is almost always a cookie.

choices.text: A name you invent has to begin with `X-` to be accepted by proxies
choices.why: That convention was withdrawn; proxies pass through what they do not know.

choices.text: The order of the headers decides which one wins when two disagree
choices.why: Order carries no meaning for headers generally.

prompt: Why does a browser claim in its `User-Agent` to be several browsers it is not?
hint: Somebody was checking the string.

choices.text: The format requires each engine listed
choices.why: There is no such format; the line is free text and always was.

choices.text: Sites refused what they did not know
choices.why: Each new browser claimed the ones before it, and the claims accumulated.

choices.text: Proxies pick a version from it
choices.why: A cache uses the address and whatever `Vary` names.
Nothing certifies browsers, and the string would not be where it was recorded.

prompt: A browser sends `Accept-Language: pt-BR,pt;q=0.9,en;q=0.8` and the server has English and Spanish. What should it serve?
hint: A preference that cannot be met is not an error.

choices.why: The first line of the list it can actually satisfy.
English is one of the three, and `406` is nearly always the wrong answer anyway.
Nothing in the mechanism measures how close two languages are.
The choice is made per request, from that request's own list.

prompt: A site is reported as showing the wrong language for some visitors, and never for the team that built it. What is the likely cause?
hint: Ask who visits first.

choices.text: A cache stores one answer per address
choices.why: `Vary` is what tells the cache the header is part of the key.
The order is a setting and is stable for a given browser.

choices.text: The server reads the list backwards
choices.why: That would be wrong for everybody, including the team.

choices.text: They have an old copy stored
choices.why: That would be reported as a stale page rather than as a wrong language.

prompt: Fill the blank: the response header that tells a cache which request header the answer depended on is `___`.
hint: Four letters, and leaving it out is the defect above.

prompt: Why do most sites choose language with an address like `/pt/precos` rather than from the header?
hint: Think about sending somebody a link.

choices.why: Browsers send it consistently; reliability is not the objection.

choices.text: A link then carries the language
choices.why: A header choice is invisible, unshareable and hard to argue with.
Nothing is being withdrawn; both mechanisms are current.

choices.text: The header is unreadable before decrypting
choices.why: The server decrypts everything it receives; that is not a cost here.

prompt: For which of these is negotiation a good fit? Choose all that apply.
hint: It works where there is a right answer the visitor has no opinion about.

choices.text: Choosing an image format the browser can decode
choices.why: Half the bytes, same picture, nobody asked.

choices.text: Choosing a compression the browser can unpack
choices.why: The cheapest improvement on the whole list.

choices.text: Answering one address as a page for a browser and as data for a program
choices.why: A deliberate use, with real costs in caching and debugging.

choices.text: Choosing which of two prices to show a visitor
choices.why: That is a decision somebody has to be able to see and change.

choices.text: Deciding whether a visitor is allowed to see a document
choices.why: Access has nothing to do with what formats a caller accepts.

prompt: Which of the three promises is the one people most often leave out?
hint: Reading is invisible. Something else is not.

choices.why: Providers have injected advertising into pages passing through.
This is the one everybody names first.

choices.text: Identity — the answerer holds the name
choices.why: Commonly known, and the certificate makes it visible in the address bar.
Not a promise of TLS at all; a newer transport addresses it separately.

prompt: An observer on the café network watches an HTTPS connection. What do they learn?
hint: The line runs between which site and which page.

choices.text: Which site, when, and roughly how much
choices.why: Enough to know you were there and for how long.

choices.text: Which page, but not the contents
choices.why: The path is inside the encryption and is not visible.

choices.text: That encrypted traffic left, and no more
choices.why: The address and, in nearly all deployments, the name are visible.

choices.text: The whole request, given the certificate
choices.why: A certificate is public and holds no key that decrypts anything.

prompt: Fill the blank: agreeing on a cipher, presenting a certificate and establishing a key costs round ___ before the first byte of the request moves.
hint: The thing lesson three taught you to count.

prompt: A browser refuses a certificate. Which of these are reasons it might? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three distinct problems, and they are not equally serious.

choices.text: The dates on it have passed
choices.why: Usually an automatic renewal that stopped working.

choices.text: It is valid, and for a different name than the one asked for
choices.why: Indistinguishable from the real thing to a browser, so it refuses.

choices.text: The chain ends at an issuer the browser's list does not contain
choices.why: Sometimes an employer's own root, sometimes something else entirely.

choices.text: The page it protects loads a script over plain HTTP
choices.why: A real problem, and browsers report it as mixed content rather than a bad certificate.

choices.text: The site is new and has not yet been reviewed by the issuer
choices.why: Nothing reviews a site; the certificate attests to control of a name.

prompt: A page served over HTTPS loads one script over plain HTTP. Why is that worse than it looks?
hint: Ask what a script is allowed to do.

choices.text: The page falls back to plain HTTP
choices.why: The rest of the page keeps its own connections and their protection.

choices.text: Changing it in transit gains the page
choices.why: Which makes the padlock on the surrounding page an active lie.
The certificate is untouched by what the page chooses to fetch.

choices.text: The script is served more slowly
choices.why: True, and trivial beside what it actually costs.

prompt: A wrong `301` was published and fixed five minutes later. Why are some visitors still sent to the wrong address?
hint: Ask whether a request is reaching you at all.

choices.why: You cannot serve a correction to somebody who has stopped asking.

choices.text: A search engine sends them there
choices.why: That also happens, and it does not explain visitors typing the address.

choices.text: Their provider's cache is holding it
choices.why: A cache in the middle expires; a stored permanent redirect may not.
Nothing about HTTP propagates; the next request would get the new answer.

prompt: What does `303` do that `302` does not reliably do?
hint: It is the one that makes refreshing a form result harmless.

choices.text: It leaves the original address in the bar
choices.why: The bar shows the destination for every redirect in the family.

choices.text: It turns the next request into a `GET`
choices.why: Which is what makes a form result reloadable and shareable.
That is the permanent codes, and `303` is not one of them.
It does the opposite: the body is dropped along with the method.

prompt: Fill the blank: ship a new redirect as a `302` first, because a `___` is stored by the browser and a mistake cannot be reached to correct.
hint: The permanent one.

prompt: Put this redirect chain in the order the browser walks it.
hint: It starts with what somebody typed.
items: `https://www.example.com/pt/` — the language, and the page at last
trap: It is tempting to put the language first, because it is the most visible difference. It is last: each rule was added by a different person on a different day, and the visitor pays for all of them in order.

prompt: A site shows *too many redirects* and the application code contains no redirect at all. Where should you look?
hint: Several layers can issue one.

choices.text: The server, the framework, the front
choices.why: A `www` rule and an anti-`www` rule, each correct alone.

choices.text: The browser, replaying an old one
choices.why: That sends you somewhere wrong rather than round in a circle.
The message is about a loop; raising a limit would change the message alone.
A name mismatch produces a warning, and no redirect at all.

prompt: What changed between HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2?
hint: Ask what a `404` means in each.

choices.text: The methods and codes were replaced by a numbered set
choices.why: Methods and codes are untouched; that is the striking thing about the change.

choices.text: How it is written, and what shares a connection
choices.why: Same meanings, binary encoding, many streams at once.
Browsers require it in practice; the specification does not.
Headers are compressed with a table, and the names are unchanged.

prompt: Why did combining many small files into one big file stop being a good idea?
hint: It was a workaround. For what?

choices.why: There is no such refusal; large files load like any other.

choices.text: It was beating a queue that is gone
choices.why: Many exchanges now share a connection, so the small files cost nothing extra.
Compression usually does better with more material, not worse.

choices.text: One change invalidates the whole file
choices.why: That is a real cost of the technique and was true before the change too.

prompt: Fill the blank: HTTP/3 is carried over ___ rather than over TCP, so that a lost packet stalls one exchange instead of all of them.
hint: Three letters, and it was already passing through the middleboxes.

prompt: HTTP/2 removed the queue at its own layer. What did that uncover?
hint: The layer underneath still delivers in order.

choices.why: The streams are independent to HTTP and not to what carries them.
That limit was a workaround for the queue and stopped mattering with it.
A real complication of the design, and not what the queue was hiding.

choices.text: The cost of the encryption agreement
choices.why: It is agreed once per connection, not once per stream.

prompt: Match each version to what it introduced.
hint: One of them is a change of transport.

pairs.right: A connection kept open, and a required `Host`
A binary encoding, with many exchanges sharing one connection
A new transport, where each exchange is ordered on its own

right_distractors: A mandatory encryption layer with no way to switch it off
A replacement set of methods and status codes

prompt: A form submission is answered with `303` pointing at a result page. What has that bought?
hint: Think about what pressing refresh does afterwards.

choices.text: The result page reloads and shares safely
choices.why: Three characters, and the *do not press refresh* warning is unnecessary.

choices.text: The form is resubmitted in the background
choices.why: The opposite: the point is that it is not submitted again.

choices.text: The browser keeps the form's values
choices.why: Browsers do that on their own, and it is unrelated to the code.
The `POST` itself is unchanged; what changed is what refresh repeats.

prompt: Which response tells you the failure is behind a proxy, and that the thing behind it never answered?
hint: Two of the 500s name a place. One of those names a timeout.

choices.why: That one is about this server being unavailable on purpose.
A gateway timeout: the proxy waited and nothing came.
That says something threw here, with no claim about where here is.
Close, and it means the answer was nonsense rather than absent.

prompt: A chain goes plain HTTP, then HTTPS, then the `www` name, then the language prefix. How many round trips are spent before the request that returns the page?
hint: Count the redirects, not the addresses.

prompt: Which of these belong in a response that carries a body? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three of them describe the body itself.

choices.why: What the bytes are, which nothing downstream can work out alone.
How many bytes, unless the body is being sent in chunks.

choices.text: `Vary`, when the answer depended on a request header
choices.why: Without it a cache files every variant under one key.
A request header: it names the site being asked for.
A request header too: it is the asking half of negotiation.

prompt: A client library retries automatically on `5xx` and not on `4xx`. Why is that arrangement sensible?
hint: Ask which family says the caller did something wrong.

choices.why: They do not resolve themselves; they need the caller to change something.

choices.text: The same wrong request, the same answer
choices.why: `5xx` may be transient; `4xx` is a statement about what was sent.
Idempotence is a property of methods, and not of response families.

choices.text: A `4xx` is cached, so a retry reads the copy
choices.why: Caching is decided by headers, and would be the same for both families.

prompt: Fill the blank: because the protocol itself remembers nothing between requests, every request carries what is needed to answer it — which is why it is described as ___.
hint: The word from the first reading of this lesson.

prompt: You are choosing the method for an action that marks an order as paid. What is the question worth asking?
hint: The method is a message to software you will never meet.

choices.text: Whether it changes data others read
choices.why: A real design question, and not the one the method answers.

choices.text: What a proxy or a retry assumes
choices.why: The word is a promise to software you did not write.
Convenience is not what the caller downstream is reading.
A body can be attached where it is needed; it does not decide the word.

prompt: What does a padlock in the address bar prove about the site behind it?
hint: One thing, and it is narrower than people assume.

choices.text: That the answerer controls the name
choices.why: It says nothing about whether they are honest or careful.
A certificate proving that exists, costs money, and is not this one.

choices.text: That your data is handled properly
choices.why: Nothing in the protocol reaches past the far end of the connection.

choices.text: That the site is not new
choices.why: One can be issued in about a minute, free, this morning.

prompt: On a link with 100 ms of latency, how many milliseconds does an extra two-round-trip negotiation add before the first byte of the request moves?
hint: One round trip costs one latency.

prompt: Put these in the order they happen for a fresh HTTPS request.
hint: Two of them are finished before any HTTP is spoken.
items: The two sides agree on a version and a cipher
The server presents a certificate and the client checks it
The response comes back with a status line and headers
trap: The tempting order puts the request first, because it is what you asked for. It is third: the connection has to be negotiated before a single character of HTTP can be sent, and that is what the extra round trips are.

prompt: A team is told to reduce requests on a site that is served over HTTP/2. What is wrong with the advice?
hint: The advice was right for a different version.

choices.text: Requests are cheap; connections are not
choices.why: Many exchanges share one connection, so the count matters far less.

choices.text: Reducing them means combining files again
choices.why: True, and a cost rather than the reason the advice is out of date.
A team decides how many things a page asks for.
Header compression helps, and it is not the mechanism that made the advice stale.

prompt: Which pair of a code and a method fits *this was created, and it is over there*?
hint: One of the codes has a companion header.

choices.why: Created, and the header says where it went.
That is a fine pair for a replacement that has nothing to report.

choices.text: `POST`, then `200` with the address in the body
choices.why: Works, and throws away the code and the header that were built for it.
A redirect after a fetch, which is not a creation at all.
